prompt.brief: Design one-to-one and group messaging with delivery, ordering, presence, and history so users can send a message to a conversation reliably at scale.
successSignals: Define the source of truth for message log and conversation membership and make retries idempotent.
Use bounded, partitioned state to meet 100M daily users and 1M messages per second and message acknowledgement p95 <=150ms.
Separate the critical request path from fanout, push notifications, search, and media.
Explain consistency, failure recovery, authorization, observability, and a degraded mode.

functional: Support the core workflow to send a message to a conversation.
Expose status, results, and freshness appropriate to one-to-one and group messaging with delivery, ordering, presence, and history.
Support authorization, validation, updates, deletion, and recovery semantics.
nonFunctional: Meet message acknowledgement p95 <=150ms under normal load.
Scale to 100M daily users and 1M messages per second without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 100M daily users and 1M messages per second
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

dataFlow.title: Accept send a message to a conversation
dataFlow.description: The One-to-one gateway authenticates the caller, validates the request, applies tenant policy and idempotency, then routes it to the owning service.

dataFlow.title: Commit the durable state
dataFlow.description: The One-to-one service records the accepted state and version before acknowledging the client.

dataFlow.description: A durable outbox publishes committed One-to-one events; consumers deduplicate by event ID and track offsets.

dataFlow.description: Partitioned workers consume One-to-one events, update the serving projection, and expose lag or watermark metadata.

dataFlow.title: Serve and recover asynchronously
dataFlow.description: Serving reads use the One-to-one projection; replay, repair, export, and slow work remain off the request path.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the One-to-one commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional One-to-one writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return One-to-one version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition One-to-one by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound One-to-one work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for One-to-one projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable One-to-one projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable One-to-one records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure One-to-one latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.

rubric.description: The answer defines the send a message to a conversation workflow, scale, latency, durability, and failure contract.
Entities and keys support one-to-one and group messaging with delivery, ordering, presence, and history, authorization, privacy, and lifecycle changes.
Partitioning, cache behavior, queues, backpressure, and hot-key handling are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded reads, and observability protect committed state.
The candidate can explain One-to-one consistency, push/pull, managed services, and the scale boundary.
